questions.q: What are the three fact table types this lesson introduces?
options: Transaction, periodic snapshot, and accumulating snapshot
Star, snowflake, and galaxy
Additive, semi-additive, and non-additive
Staging, dimension, and bridge
questions.explain: Microsoft's dimensional modeling guidance for Fabric names exactly three fact table types by their load and update behavior: transaction, periodic snapshot, and accumulating snapshot.

questions.q: What is the defining trait of a transaction fact table?
options: One row per business event, inserted once and never updated except to correct an error
One row per fixed time interval regardless of whether anything happened
One row per process instance, updated repeatedly as it progresses
A table that contains no measure columns at all
questions.explain: A transaction fact table records events as they happen — a sales order line, a call, a click — with each row fully known and immutable at insert time.

questions.q: Why can't you validly sum an inventory periodic snapshot measure across multiple days?
options: Because the measure is semi-additive — it can be summed across entities like products, but summing it across time periods double-counts stock that was simply carried forward
Because periodic snapshot tables don't allow the SUM() function
Because inventory measures are always stored as text
Because periodic snapshot tables have no date dimension key
questions.explain: An inventory balance sampled nightly represents a point-in-time state, not a new event each day — adding it across days produces a meaningless number.

questions.q: What makes the ETL load pattern for an accumulating snapshot fact table different from a transaction fact table?
options: It requires an UPDATE that finds the existing row for a process instance and advances it to the next milestone, rather than only inserting new rows
It cannot be loaded with T-SQL at all
It only ever loads once per year
It has no dimension keys, only measures
questions.explain: Because one row tracks a process instance across multiple stages, the load has to locate that row and update it in place — a fundamentally different pattern than the insert-only load a transaction table uses.

questions.q: A support ticket moves through "opened," "assigned," "in progress," and "closed," and you want to measure how long it sat in each stage. Which fact table type fits?
options: Accumulating snapshot — one row per ticket, updated as it reaches each milestone
Transaction — one row per ticket, inserted once and never touched again
Periodic snapshot — one row per ticket per day regardless of status
Factless — a row with no measures at all
questions.explain: Tracking a single process instance through a well-defined sequence of milestones, and measuring durations between them, is exactly what an accumulating snapshot fact table is designed for.
